attempts_list.fix: LEAKED, and not a documented residual — it is the T-0239 fix-round review's own FK exclusion being wrong in the same way the length exclusion was wrong. THREAT_MODEL.md's 2026-09-17 amendment records that exclusion as costing nothing, and internal/classify/classify.go's comment on `raisableUnknown` states the claim explicitly: 'A genuinely personal FK-linked column is still reached by every other pass -- a name hit, a value validator, or FK propagation once one end is masked on real evidence.' This schema is the disproof: there is no name hit (the column name is Amharic), no value validator hit (the dictionary does not carry the names), and nothing to propagate, because the rail that would have supplied the 'real evidence' is the one being skipped. Turning a column into an FK child is a one-line schema change an attacker or an ordinary dimension-table author makes for free, and it converts a masked column into a copied one. The exclusion exists for a real problem — a rail-masked child whose unmasked parent leaves the join in disagreement, so internal/load's NOT VALID + VALIDATE dies with the target half loaded (regressions/031) — but the answer to that is to mask both ends, not to copy both. Fix: in `unknownColumnsBesideCertain`, when a raisable column is at either end of a validated FK, raise BOTH ends together under the same category (the rail already walks the schema, and `indexFKColumns` already knows the pairs), so the join stays in agreement and the values stop crossing; where the partner end is itself excluded for another reason (unique index, two-letter codes, type conflict), refuse the run at exit 12 naming the pair with the `--unmask` escape, the way internal/plan already refuses a unique-indexed column free_text cannot fill. Silently copying the pair is the one outcome that should not be available. Pin this schema (native-script FK child + certain email neighbour, parent with no certain column) as a regression fixture; regressions/031 pins only the safe direction.

attempts_list.fix: LEAKED, 300 national identifiers verbatim under exit 0, and I mark it documented because THREAT_MODEL.md's 2026-09-17 T-0240 amendment names this exact mechanism as accepted: 'The exemption now stays unconditional for a column internal/classify has already decided is a surrogate key or a validated foreign-key child whose parent stayed unmasked (Decision.NeverMasked, carried the same way the three corroboration fields are).' T1's own ID sentence does NOT cover it — that sentence is scoped to 'a table with no other column decided possible or above under a person-identifying category', and this table has a masked phone. The residual is named but it is worth narrowing, because the carve-out's justification does not stretch this far. Its stated reason is `order_id`: a column whose values ARE its parent surrogate key's, copied verbatim, must not lose its exemption because of an unrelated `email` elsewhere in the table. That reason is about a MIRROR of a key, not about a natural primary key that is itself the identifier, and the diagnostic above shows the project already agrees the two are different: rename the column `ssn` and the same schema is refused at exit 12. Fix: split the carve-out in two. Keep it unconditional for a validated FK child whose parent stayed unmasked (the `order_id` case the regression pins). For a column that is never-masked only because it is the table's own surrogate key, let `corroboratedForSeq` defeat the exemption as it does for every other dense column, and score the ratio; a dense block of nine-digit values in a primary key beside a masked personal neighbour is a payroll or benefits import keyed on the national identifier, not a generated sequence. The natural outcome is the plan refusal the named control already produces — exit 12 naming the column with the `--unmask` escape — since a personal primary key cannot be masked without breaking the key anyway. Pin this schema (dense national-ID block as the table's own primary key, masked phone neighbour) as a regression; testdata/regressions/018-023 and 032-034 all put the identifier in a non-key column.

Nothing forces it, but pg_basebackup into a second directory is the ordinary way to stand a standby up beside its primary, and any co-hosted pair disagrees by necessity. Line 99 then leans on the standby rail to cover this case ("a standby whose data_directory genuinely differs ... is still caught") while line 99 also says "A --target the operator named is unaffected by either rail" — so for a named target nothing at all covers it, and the guarantee in line 81 is silently broken. Two changes. (1) Make the standby fact feed the identity rather than only the header: when Source.Replica reports Standby == true, data_directory joins the start time in clusterIDDifferenceUnreliableField for that run — a standby's data directory is no more evidence of a different cluster than its start time is. That is a one-line change to the field predicate plus plumbing ReplicaStatus.Standby into SetSourceCluster, and it costs nothing when the source is not a standby. (2) Cheaper and strictly decisive where the role can read it: when the source is a standby, compare pg_stat_wal_receiver's sender_host/sender_port (already read by Source.Replica) against the target's endpoint, and when they resolve to the same server report SameCluster true outright — today lazyslice reads the primary's address and then throws it away into a header string. Regression pin: extend internal/pg/cluster_test.go's TestAStandbysStartTimeDisagreementWithoutSystemIdentifierIsUnknown with a case where data_directory is filled and differs on both sides and the source is known to be a standby, asserting unknown rather than "different".

attempts_list.fix: Nothing was destroyed, but read the refusal code: the run was stopped by rule 5 (emptiness), NOT by rule 1. Rule 1's sameCatalog arm (internal/pg/target.go:290) requires currentDB == source.Database AND (clusterUnknown || equal system identifiers || (clusterKnown && clusterSame)); with data_directory readable and differing, clusterKnown is true and clusterSame is false, so the arm is skipped and the target's endpoint differs, so sameEndpoint is false too. The source's own database, reached through its primary, passed rule 1. The only thing between that and a drop is the production database happening to hold rows — so the mid-migration shape T-0222 built the fail-closed same-name arm for (an empty, freshly cut-over production database carrying the source's name) walks straight through it. The fix is the same as the variant above: stop believing a data_directory disagreement when the source is a standby, which restores clusterUnknown and with it the same-name refusal. Worth a dedicated pin in internal/pg/gate_integration_test.go asserting CodeSameDatabase, not CodeNotEmpty, for a same-named target on a standby's primary.

attempts_list.attack: Run lease, defeat by losing the holder: terminate the backend holding the lease while run A is stalled between the gate and the load (a DBA's idle-in-transaction reaper, a pooler restart, a laptop sleep or a dropped connection — the lease connection sits `idle in transaction` for the whole run by design), then start run B. attempts_list.fix: THREAT_MODEL.md T2's residual bullet claims exactly what this breaks: "no two lazyslice runs take one target apart together." The lease is taken once, before the gate, and never looked at again: internal/pg/lease.go holds a transaction-scoped advisory lock open on one connection for the whole run, and nothing downstream asks whether that connection is still alive. Losing it needs no adversary — an `idle in transaction` session for the length of a snapshot is precisely what server-side reapers, pgbouncer restarts and NAT timeouts kill, and lazyslice's own comment notes it disarms idle_in_transaction_session_timeout only *locally*, which does not stop pg_terminate_backend. Fix: re-assert the lease where the run already stops to re-check the target. load's recheckWholeTarget (internal/load/load.go:508) is the natural place and is already a transaction on the target under the lease: add a `SELECT pg_try_advisory_xact_lock($key)` probe there that expects to FAIL (someone else, or still us) — or better, have internal/pg export a Lease.Alive(ctx) that confirms the lease connection is still the one holding classid/objid in pg_locks, and call it before the first drop and before each dropOne. A lease that has evaporated must be a refusal (load.refused.lease_lost), never a fall-through — the same rule internal/core/run.go already applies at acquisition ("A lease that cannot be taken is a refusal, never a fall-through"). Secondary defect worth its own task: run A surfaced a raw SQLSTATE 23505 as "lazyslice failed for a reason it has no code for", so the one observable symptom of a defeated lease is an uncoded crash.

attempts_list.fix: Documented residual, THREAT_MODEL.md T2, the bullet "**The residual, stated rather than closed.**": "Neither control stops an application from writing to the target: an advisory lock coordinates only clients that ask for it ... What is closed is narrower and is the thing the review found: no lazyslice run destroys a table on a verdict that has stopped being true, and no two lazyslice runs take one target apart together." Nothing was destroyed and no second lazyslice run took part. But the exit-0 half that T-0242 was filed to close is only closed for an unmarked target: a reload — the ordinary daily case, since any target lazyslice has written once is marker-bound forever after — still exits 0 and writes `complete` over a database that is part fake and part production, which is the operator-facing half of the round-4 finding. The round-5 note in recheckWholeTarget's comment is right that the marker-bound path cannot reuse the gate's rule-5 verdict (there isn't one) and right that refusing on "a table the plan no longer has" would false-positive on a legitimately full target. Neither argument requires silence: on the marker-bound path, run the same ProbeEmptiness sweep and, for each occupied table that is neither in the plan nor recorded in the marker's own table list from the previous run, print a warning naming it (target.warn.unknown_tables) and degrade the exit to non-zero rather than refusing. That needs the marker to record the tables the run wrote, which it should record anyway — it is the only thing that makes "this database is mine" a checkable claim rather than a single bound row. Failing that, amend the T2 residual bullet, which currently explains the residual as a writer "blocked by the lock until then" writing "into the fresh table lazyslice created": a table created outside the plan is never locked and never rechecked, so the writer is not blocked at all and the rows are not lazyslice's own.
